lines.display: Hi! Today we learn about **animal life**.
Not one animal — all of them.
We will see how they live around us.
You already see most of them every day.
The cow, the crow, the bee at a flower.
Let's go!
We will answer four questions together.
First, how do plants and animals need each other?
Second, how do we group an animal by what it eats?
Third, how does all this eating join every living thing?
Last, how does an animal's baby arrive?
And who looks after that baby?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Our Four Questions

lines.display: Every living thing needs food.
You need food.
A goat needs food.
A tree needs food too.
So where does all this food come from?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Every Living Thing Needs Food

cards.title: Only Plants Make Their Own Food

lines.display: Only **plants** make their own food.
No other living thing can do it.
Remember the leaf, from our plant chapter?
The leaf makes the food for the whole plant.
The plant does not go anywhere to find it.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Only Plants Make Their Own Food

lines.display: Now think about an animal.
Can a cow make its own food inside itself?
No, a cow cannot.
Can a lion make its own food?
No, a lion cannot.
**No animal** can make its own food.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: No Animal Can Do This

lines.display: So every animal must take food from somewhere else.
A cow eats grass.
Grass is a plant.
So the cow takes plant food straight from the plant.
We say the cow gets its food **directly** from plants.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Cow Takes It Straight

cards.title: The Lion Takes It Through a Deer

lines.display: Now think about a lion.
A lion eats a deer.
And that deer ate grass.
So the plant food went into the deer first.
Then it went from the deer into the lion.
We say the lion gets its food **indirectly** from plants.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Lion Takes It Through a Deer

lines.display: Both animals live on plant food in the end.
One takes it **directly**.
One takes it **indirectly**.
Keep these two words safe.
We will use them again later.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Directly and Indirectly

question.prompt: A cow eats grass. How does the cow get its food?

hint.display: Grass is a plant, and the cow eats it itself.

grading.correctAnswerText: Directly from plants
grading.reason: Yes! The cow eats the plant itself. That is directly from plants.

question.prompt: Choose all the sentences that are true about a lion's food.

options.text: The lion makes its own food.
Plant food reaches the lion through the deer.
The lion takes its food directly from plants.

hint.display: Think about what the deer ate before the lion came.

grading.correctAnswerText: The lion eats a deer.; That deer ate grass.; Plant food reaches the lion through the deer.
grading.reason: Yes! No animal makes its own food. The lion's food comes through the deer.

lines.display: Animals take more than food from plants.
They take the **oxygen** they breathe.
Every breath you take has oxygen in it.
And plants give that oxygen out.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Animals Take More Than Food

lines.display: Plants give animals many other useful things too.
Shade to sit in.
Branches to build a nest on.
Fruit to eat.
So the plant gives, and the animal takes.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Other Useful Things

cards.title: Does the Plant Get Nothing Back?

lines.display: Right now you may be thinking something.
The plant gives and gives.
The animal only takes.
The plant gets nothing back.
That is not true.
Let's see what the plant gets.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Does the Plant Get Nothing Back?

lines.display: Remember your lungs, from our body chapter?
You breathe air in, then you breathe air out.
When you breathe out, a gas comes out of you.
That gas is called **carbon dioxide**.
Every animal breathes out carbon dioxide.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Gas You Breathe Out

lines.display: The plant needs that carbon dioxide.
The plant takes it and uses it.
And the plant gives out **oxygen**.
You breathe that oxygen in.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Plant Needs That Gas

lines.display: Picture two arrows between an animal and a plant.
One arrow comes out of the animal.
That arrow says **carbon dioxide**.
One arrow comes out of the plant.
That arrow says **oxygen**.

visual.title: Two Arrows
visual.description: Two labelled arrows between an animal and a plant - carbon dioxide going one way, oxygen coming back.

interactive.label: Tap an arrow to see which one gives out that gas

cards.title: Each One Gives What the Other Needs

lines.display: Look at those two arrows again.
The animal gives out the gas the plant needs.
The plant gives out the gas the animal needs.
So the giving goes both ways.
That is the first thing the plant gets back.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Each One Gives What the Other Needs

question.prompt:
True or false?

Animals breathe out oxygen.

hint.display: Look again at the arrow that comes out of the animal.

grading.correctAnswerText: False
grading.reason: Right, that is false. Animals breathe out carbon dioxide. Plants give out oxygen.

question.prompt: Choose all the sentences that match our two arrows.

options.text: The animal gives out carbon dioxide.
The plant gives out carbon dioxide.
The animal breathes the oxygen in.
The plant breathes the oxygen in.

hint.display: One arrow comes out of the animal. One comes out of the plant.

grading.correctAnswerText: The animal gives out carbon dioxide.; The plant gives out oxygen.; The animal breathes the oxygen in.
grading.reason: Yes! Each one gives out the gas the other one needs.

lines.display: Before the next thing, one new word.
**Pollen**.
Pollen is the fine powder a flower makes.
It looks like yellow dust on your finger.
A plant needs its pollen to make new plants.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: A New Word: Pollen

lines.display: But the pollen must first reach another flower.
Only then can new plants be made.
And a flower cannot walk.
It cannot carry its pollen across to another flower.
So an animal does the carrying for it.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Pollen Must Travel

lines.display: Stand near a pumpkin or mustard flower in the morning.
Count the bees going in and out.
The bee comes for the sweet juice.
Pollen sticks to its body.
The bee flies to the next flower.
It leaves some pollen there.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Watch the Bees

cards.title: The Bee Is Not Trying to Help

lines.display: The bee is not trying to help the plant.
It came only for food.
But the plant got its pollen carried.
That is the second thing the plant gets back.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Bee Is Not Trying to Help

lines.display: Animals carry seeds for plants too.
Walk through a patch of long grass in a park.
Then sit down and look at your socks.
Little seeds are stuck all over them.
You just carried them away from the plant.
Remember how a seed travels, from our plant chapter?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Seeds on Your Socks

lines.display: So this carrying does two jobs for the plant.
It is how a plant makes new plants.
It is how a plant's seeds reach new ground.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Carrying Does Two Jobs

cards.title: A Word for Making New Ones

lines.display: Making new young ones like this has a name.
We call it **reproduction**.
A plant reproduces when it makes new plants.
You will meet that word again later, with animals.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: A Word for Making New Ones

lines.display: People need both plants and animals as well.
Look at what we get from the two of them.
Food, clothes, wood and honey.
All of it comes from plants and animals together.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: People Need Them Both

lines.display: So the animal needs the plant.
And the plant needs the animal.
This two-way give-and-take has a name.
We call it **interdependence**.
You can also say it in plain words.
Plants and animals **depend on each other**.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Interdependence

lines.display: Take the plants away.
Then the animals have no food and no oxygen.
Now take the animals away.
Then nobody breathes out carbon dioxide for the plant.
And nobody carries its pollen and its seeds.

visual.title: Take One Side Away
visual.description: The four things plant and animal give each other, with one side greyed out at a time so the arrows that die can be seen.

question.prompt: Plants and animals depend on each other. We call this ___.

hint.display: It is our long word for a two-way give-and-take.

grading.correctAnswerText: interdependence
grading.reason: Yes! Interdependence means plants and animals depend on each other.

question.prompt: Take all the animals away. Choose all the things the plants would lose.

options.text: The bees that carry their pollen.
The animals that carry their seeds.

hint.display: Remember, a plant still makes its own food by itself.

grading.correctAnswerText: The carbon dioxide they need.; The bees that carry their pollen.; The animals that carry their seeds.
grading.reason: Yes! No gas comes back, and nobody carries the pollen or seeds.

cards.title: Neither Can Live Without the Other

lines.display: So neither side could live without the other.
The plant needs the animal.
The animal needs the plant.
That is the whole idea of **interdependence**.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Neither Can Live Without the Other

lines.display: Animals do not all eat the same thing.
So we put them into groups.
One rule decides the group.
**What does this animal eat?**
Ask that about any animal and you get its group.
There are three groups, and we will meet each one.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: One Question Sorts Every Animal

lines.display: Some animals eat only plant food.
Only plant food, nothing else.
We call them **herbivores**.
Herbivore just means plant eater.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Group One: Plant Eaters

lines.display: You know many plant eaters already.
A cow, a buffalo, a goat, a deer, a rabbit.
An elephant and a giraffe as well.
Every one of them eats plant food and nothing else.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Plant Eaters You Know

cards.title: Two Kinds of Teeth, Two Jobs

lines.display: A plant eater's teeth match its food.
It has two kinds of teeth.
Each kind has one job.
The front teeth are wide with a sharp edge.
They cut a mouthful of grass away easily.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Two Kinds of Teeth, Two Jobs

lines.display: The back teeth are flat and strong.
They grind that mouthful until it is soft.
Remember from our food chapter?
Food must be chewed well before it goes down.
Those flat teeth do that chewing.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Grinding Teeth

cards.title: The Cow That Chews All Day

lines.display: Watch a cow sitting in the shade.
Its mouth is moving.
Come back ten minutes later, and it is still moving.
Is the cow eating all day?
No, it is doing something called **chewing the cud**.
Let's follow one mouthful of grass through it.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one mouthful of grass through a cow's two rounds of chewing
conceptGroup.title: Chewing the Cud

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Cow That Chews All Day

lines.display: First the cow eats the grass and swallows it.
It does not chew the grass much at all.
Down goes the mouthful, almost whole.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one mouthful of grass through a cow's two rounds of chewing
conceptGroup.title: Chewing the Cud

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Step One: Swallow It

cards.title: Step Two: Bring It Back Up

lines.display: Later the cow brings that same grass back up.
Back up into its mouth it comes.
This is the part most people never notice.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one mouthful of grass through a cow's two rounds of chewing
conceptGroup.title: Chewing the Cud

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Step Two: Bring It Back Up

lines.display: Now the cow chews the grass properly.
Its tongue moves the food about inside the mouth.
The tongue keeps doing this all through the chewing.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one mouthful of grass through a cow's two rounds of chewing
conceptGroup.title: Chewing the Cud

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Step Three: Chew It Well

lines.display: Then the cow swallows the grass a second time.
Now the food is soft and well chewed.
And that mouthful is finished.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one mouthful of grass through a cow's two rounds of chewing
conceptGroup.title: Chewing the Cud

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Step Four: Swallow It Again

lines.display: Let's see the whole thing in one look.
The food goes down, then comes back up.
It gets chewed well, then goes down again.
That second round of chewing takes a long time.
This is why a cow looks like it chews all day.
A buffalo does this too.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one mouthful of grass through a cow's two rounds of chewing
conceptGroup.title: Chewing the Cud

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Two Rounds for One Mouthful

question.prompt: In chewing the cud, which step comes right after 'Bring up'?

hint.display: The grass has just come back into the cow's mouth.

grading.correctAnswerText: Chew well
grading.reason: Yes! After bringing it up, the cow chews the grass well.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one mouthful of grass through a cow's two rounds of chewing
conceptGroup.title: Chewing the Cud

question.prompt: Choose all the steps we used for chewing the cud.

hint.display: Think about the very first thing the cow did with the grass.

grading.correctAnswerText: Swallow; Bring up; Chew well; Swallow again
grading.reason: Yes! Swallow, bring up, chew well, swallow again. The food went down first.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one mouthful of grass through a cow's two rounds of chewing
conceptGroup.title: Chewing the Cud

lines.display: Notice the very first step again.
The cow swallowed the grass before chewing it.
So chewing the cud is not just chewing a long time.
The food went down first, and then came back up.
That first swallow is what makes it chewing the cud.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Food Went Down First

lines.display: Some plant eaters eat in a different way.
A rabbit, a rat and a squirrel have large front teeth.
Those front teeth are big and sharp.
Their food is hard: nuts, seeds and hard fruit.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Gnawing

lines.display: So they take one small bite, then another, then another.
They use those large front teeth for every bite.
Taking many small bites like this is called **gnawing**.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Many Small Bites

lines.display: Not every plant eater reaches its food with its teeth.
Look at an elephant.
Its **trunk** does that work.
The trunk pulls a plant up out of the ground.
It tears food away from a tree.
It carries the food to the mouth.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Elephant's Trunk

lines.display: The trunk even sucks up water.
Then it sprays that water over the elephant's body.
The teeth do none of that work.
An elephant's teeth only cut and grind the food.
And they do that once it is inside the mouth.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Trunk Does More

lines.display: A giraffe has a different tool.
Its neck is very long.
Good leaves grow high up a tree.
They are far above the ground.
The giraffe's long neck reaches them.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Giraffe's Long Neck

lines.display: The second group eats flesh.
Flesh means the meat of another animal.
We call them **carnivores**.
Carnivore just means flesh eater.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Group Two: Flesh Eaters

lines.display: On land you know these ones.
Cats, wolves, tigers and lions.
The rule has not changed.
We are still asking one thing.
What does this animal eat?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Flesh Eaters on Land

lines.display: A flesh eater's teeth match its food too.
Its front teeth are sharp and pointed.
They rip the meat away.
Its back teeth are strong.
They cut through meat and bone alike.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: A Flesh Eater's Teeth

lines.display: A flesh eater has claws as well.
The claws trap the animal it has caught.
They hold it and keep it from getting free.
Claws catch and hold.
Claws do not chew.

question.prompt:
True or false?

A flesh eater uses its claws to chew its food.

hint.display: Think about what the claws do to the animal that is caught.

grading.correctAnswerText: False
grading.reason: Right, that is false. Claws catch and hold. Claws do not chew.

question.prompt: Choose all the jobs a flesh eater's teeth do.

options.text: The front teeth rip the meat away.
The back teeth cut through meat and bone.
They hold the caught animal so it cannot get free.
They grind grass until it is soft.

hint.display: One job here belongs to the claws. One belongs to a plant eater.

grading.correctAnswerText: The front teeth rip the meat away.; The back teeth cut through meat and bone.
grading.reason: Yes! Sharp front teeth rip, and strong back teeth cut through bone.

lines.display: Some flesh eaters live in water.
Sharks, pikes and piranhas are fish that eat flesh.
Their small sharp teeth grip whatever they catch.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Flesh Eaters in Water

lines.display: And some flesh eaters are small.
Snakes, frogs, lizards and chameleons all eat flesh.
They sit in this same group as the tiger.
Being small does not move them out of it.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Small Flesh Eaters Too

lines.display: Now a warning.
Many children get this one wrong.
You might think a big animal must be a flesh eater.
Or that a fierce-looking animal must be one.
That is not our rule.
Let's test it with animals you can go and see.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Careful: a Common Mistake

lines.display: Look at a buffalo on the street.
It is the biggest animal in sight.
Its mouth is full of grass all day long.
So it is a plant eater.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Buffalo on the Street

lines.display: Watch an elephant at a temple.
People hand it sugarcane, bananas and leaves.
They never hand it meat.
So it is a plant eater too.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Elephant at the Temple

lines.display: Now find a gecko on your wall.
It is smaller than your hand.
It eats nothing but insects.
So it is a flesh eater.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Gecko on Your Wall

lines.display: So size decides nothing.
Fierce looks decide nothing.
Ask the one question only.
What does this animal eat?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Size Decides Nothing

question.prompt: People hand the temple elephant sugarcane, bananas and leaves. So it is a ___.

hint.display: The food decides the group, never the size.

grading.correctAnswerText: plant eater
grading.reason: Yes! Nobody hands it meat. It eats plant food, so it is a plant eater.

question.prompt: Which of these are true about our sorting rule?

options.text: The biggest animal in sight can be a plant eater.
A very small animal can be a flesh eater.
A fierce-looking animal must be a flesh eater.

hint.display: Remember the buffalo, the temple elephant and the gecko.

grading.correctAnswerText: The biggest animal in sight can be a plant eater.; A very small animal can be a flesh eater.; The food decides the group.
grading.reason: Yes! Size and fierce looks decide nothing. Only the food decides.

lines.display: We have met two ways of eating with names.
Chewing the cud, and gnawing.
Here is the third one.
Some animals swallow their food whole.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Third Way of Eating

lines.display: A flesh eater catches an animal and eats it.
That caught animal is its **prey**.
Keep that word, because we will use it again.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: What Prey Means

cards.title: A Snake's Teeth Hold, They Do Not Chew

lines.display: A snake's teeth are made for holding its prey.
They are not made for chewing it.
So a snake does not chew at all.
The whole animal goes down.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: A Snake's Teeth Hold, They Do Not Chew

lines.display: Let's follow one caught animal all the way.
It starts in the snake's mouth.
It ends inside the snake's stomach.
Four things happen on the way.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one caught animal from the snake's mouth to its stomach
conceptGroup.title: A Snake Swallows Its Prey

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Follow One Caught Animal

lines.display: The snake catches the prey with its mouth.
It holds the prey tight.
Nothing is chewed here.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one caught animal from the snake's mouth to its stomach
conceptGroup.title: A Snake Swallows Its Prey

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Snake Catches It

lines.display: The snake's mouth has small hook-shaped parts inside it.
Those hooks pull the prey inwards.
Little by little, the prey goes in.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one caught animal from the snake's mouth to its stomach
conceptGroup.title: A Snake Swallows Its Prey

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Hooks Pull It Inwards

lines.display: Now the snake's own body muscles get to work.
They push the prey down the snake's throat.
The whole animal goes down together.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one caught animal from the snake's mouth to its stomach
conceptGroup.title: A Snake Swallows Its Prey

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Muscles Push It Down

lines.display: The prey reaches the stomach.
There the whole animal is broken down.
Remember the stomach from our food chapter?
A snake's stomach does that same job.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one caught animal from the snake's mouth to its stomach
conceptGroup.title: A Snake Swallows Its Prey

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Into the Stomach

lines.display: Let's see the snake's journey in one look.
It catches the prey and holds it tight.
The hooks pull it in and the muscles push it down.
Then the stomach breaks the whole animal down.
There is no chewing anywhere in that journey.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one caught animal from the snake's mouth to its stomach
conceptGroup.title: A Snake Swallows Its Prey

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Whole Journey

question.prompt: In the snake's journey, which step comes right after 'Catch'?

hint.display: The prey is still in the snake's mouth here.

grading.correctAnswerText: Pull in
grading.reason: Yes! The hooks pull the prey in, little by little.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one caught animal from the snake's mouth to its stomach
conceptGroup.title: A Snake Swallows Its Prey

question.prompt: Choose all the things that happen to the prey inside a snake.

options.text: The body muscles push it down the throat.
The teeth chew it into small bits.

hint.display: One of these never happens in a snake.

grading.correctAnswerText: The hooks pull it inwards.; The body muscles push it down the throat.; The stomach breaks it down.
grading.reason: Yes! Hooks pull, muscles push, the stomach breaks it down. No chewing.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one caught animal from the snake's mouth to its stomach
conceptGroup.title: A Snake Swallows Its Prey

lines.display: One snake can swallow a very big animal.
That snake is the **python**.
A python's mouth opens very wide.
It can take prey the size of a small deer.
Only the python, not every snake.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Python's Wide Mouth

lines.display: Three more mouths finish the flesh eaters.
First, the lizard.
A lizard opens its mouth wide.
Then it takes its food whole.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Lizard's Wide Mouth

lines.display: Next, the frog and the chameleon.
Each one has a long sticky tongue.
The tongue shoots out at the prey.
The prey sticks to it.
They catch their food easily this way.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Sticky Tongue

lines.display: All three of these eat flesh.
The lizard, the frog and the chameleon.
They stay here with the flesh eaters.
Remember that, because the next group is a different one.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: All Three Are Flesh Eaters

lines.display: Think about your own plate today.
Maybe there was roti, dal and a banana.
Those are plant foods.
Maybe there was milk, an egg or fish as well.
Those are animal foods.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Look at Your Own Plate

lines.display: So you eat both kinds of food.
You are not a plant eater.
You are not a flesh eater.
You are something else.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: You Eat Both Kinds

lines.display: Animals that feed on both kinds are called **omnivores**.
Omnivore just means mixed eater.
People are omnivores.
So are bears, pigs and crows.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Group Three: Mixed Eaters

lines.display: These animals take both plant food and animal food.
So they have more foods to live on.
If one food is hard to find, they eat another.
And their bodies can digest plant food and flesh alike.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Why Eating Both Helps

question.prompt:
True or false?

People are omnivores.

hint.display: Think about the roti and the egg on your plate.

grading.correctAnswerText: True
grading.reason: Yes! You eat plant food and animal food, so you are an omnivore.

question.prompt: Why does eating both kinds of food help an omnivore?

options.text: It has more foods to live on.
It does not need to chew its food.
It can make its own food inside itself.

hint.display: Think about a day when one food is hard to find.

grading.correctAnswerText: It has more foods to live on.
grading.reason: Yes! If one food is hard to find, it can eat another one.

lines.display: Here are four mixed eaters from our book.
For each one, notice both halves of what it eats.
Both halves are what put it in this group.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Four Mixed Eaters

lines.display: A **bear** has strong sharp teeth.
Those teeth can bite meat.
They can crack hard nuts and fruit too.
So a bear eats both kinds.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Bear

lines.display: An **earthworm** eats soil.
But it does not want the soil itself.
Dead plant bits and dead animal bits are mixed in it.
Those bits are its food.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Earthworm

lines.display: A **leech** fastens on to an animal.
Then it sucks that animal's blood.
It also feeds on rotting bodies and open wounds.
Some leeches feed on rotting plant matter as well.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Leech

lines.display: A **bird** eats seeds, grains and fruit.
It also eats worms, insects, fish and dead animals.
And a bird has no teeth.
It picks up all of this with its **beak**.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Bird

lines.display: Some animals eat no solid food at all.
Their food is liquid, so they drink it.
A butterfly, a honeybee and a mosquito feed this way.
None of them has teeth either.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Animals That Drink Their Food

lines.display: Each one has a long hollow tube.
That tube works like a straw.
The animal puts the tube into the liquid food.
Then it sucks the food up.
So there is no biting and no chewing.

visual.title: A Tube Like a Straw
visual.description: A straw in a glass of juice beside a butterfly's tube in a flower, with the liquid rising up both of them.

question.prompt: A butterfly has no teeth. It sucks up its food through a long hollow ___.

hint.display: It works like a straw.

grading.correctAnswerText: tube
grading.reason: Yes! The tube works like a straw, so there is no chewing.

cards.title: Both Halves of a Bird's Food

question.prompt: Which of these are true about a bird?

options.text: It eats seeds, grains and fruit.
It eats worms, insects and fish.
It has no teeth, so it uses its beak.
It eats only seeds and grain.

hint.display: A bird's food has a plant half and an animal half.

grading.correctAnswerText: It eats seeds, grains and fruit.; It eats worms, insects and fish.; It has no teeth, so it uses its beak.
grading.reason: Yes! A bird eats both halves. It picks them up with its beak.

lines.display: Butterflies, honeybees and mosquitoes are all insects.
So here is a check you can run.
Run it on any small creature you find.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Is It an Insect?

lines.display: An insect has six legs.
Its body is in three parts.
It has one pair of **feelers** on its head.
Another name for feelers is **antennae**.
And some insects have two pairs of wings.
Run that check and you will know.

visual.description: One labelled honeybee seen from above with exactly six legs, three body parts, two feelers and two pairs of wings.

lines.display: Now the mistake nearly everybody makes.
At home we call every tiny crawling thing an insect.
But small and crawly is not the check.
The legs and the three body parts are the check.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Mistake Nearly Everybody Makes

lines.display: Find an ant on the floor.
Count its legs.
Six legs.
So an ant is an insect.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Count the Ant's Legs

lines.display: Now find a spider in its web in the corner.
Count its legs.
Eight legs, not six.
And its body is not in three parts.
So a spider is not an insect at all.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Count the Spider's Legs

lines.display: A housefly on the window?
Six legs, so it is an insect.
A millipede in the damp corner near the tap?
Far too many legs to count.
So it is not an insect.
The counting settles it, and the size does not.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Two More to Check

question.prompt: A spider has eight legs. Is a spider an insect?

options.text: No, an insect has six legs.

hint.display: Small and crawly is not our check.

grading.correctAnswerText: No, an insect has six legs.
grading.reason: Yes! An insect has six legs, so a spider is not an insect.

question.prompt: Choose all the things an insect must have.

hint.display: Run the same check you would run on an ant.

grading.correctAnswerText: Six legs; A body in three parts; One pair of feelers
grading.reason: Yes! Six legs, three body parts and one pair of feelers.

lines.display: Now we know who eats what.
Let's put them in order.
We set living things out in one line.
The line follows the order of who eats whom.
Each one is food for the next one.
That line is called a **food chain**.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Putting Them in Order

lines.display: Let's build a food chain from a forest.
We will add it link by link.
Three living things, in the order of who eats whom.

conceptGroup.goal: Build one forest food chain link by link and draw its arrows
conceptGroup.title: Grass, Deer, Tiger

visual.title: Let's Build One Chain
visual.description: One food chain built link by link - grass, deer, tiger - then joined by two arrows that point at the eater.

lines.display: Start with grass.
Grass is a plant.
So it makes its own food.
That is our first link.

conceptGroup.goal: Build one forest food chain link by link and draw its arrows
conceptGroup.title: Grass, Deer, Tiger

visual.title: Let's Build One Chain
visual.description: One food chain built link by link - grass, deer, tiger - then joined by two arrows that point at the eater.

lines.display: A deer comes and eats the grass.
The grass is food for the deer.
That is our second link.

conceptGroup.goal: Build one forest food chain link by link and draw its arrows
conceptGroup.title: Grass, Deer, Tiger

visual.title: Let's Build One Chain
visual.description: One food chain built link by link - grass, deer, tiger - then joined by two arrows that point at the eater.

lines.display: A tiger comes and eats the deer.
The deer is food for the tiger.
That is our third link.
Grass, then deer, then tiger.

conceptGroup.goal: Build one forest food chain link by link and draw its arrows
conceptGroup.title: Grass, Deer, Tiger

visual.title: Let's Build One Chain
visual.description: One food chain built link by link - grass, deer, tiger - then joined by two arrows that point at the eater.

lines.display: We join the links with arrows.
The arrow has one rule.
The arrow starts at the living thing that is eaten.
It points to the one that eats it.
Eaten first, eater second.

conceptGroup.goal: Build one forest food chain link by link and draw its arrows
conceptGroup.title: Grass, Deer, Tiger

visual.title: Let's Build One Chain
visual.description: One food chain built link by link - grass, deer, tiger - then joined by two arrows that point at the eater.

lines.display: Read every arrow with these three words.
**Is eaten by.**
So grass is eaten by the deer.
And the deer is eaten by the tiger.
The arrow always points towards the one eating.

conceptGroup.goal: Build one forest food chain link by link and draw its arrows
conceptGroup.title: Grass, Deer, Tiger

visual.title: Let's Build One Chain
visual.description: One food chain built link by link - grass, deer, tiger - then joined by two arrows that point at the eater.

lines.display: Here is our whole food chain in one look.
Grass is eaten by the deer.
The deer is eaten by the tiger.
Three links, joined by two arrows.
And both arrows point the same way, towards the eater.

conceptGroup.goal: Build one forest food chain link by link and draw its arrows
conceptGroup.title: Grass, Deer, Tiger

visual.title: Let's Build One Chain
visual.description: One food chain built link by link - grass, deer, tiger - then joined by two arrows that point at the eater.

question.prompt:
True or false?

An arrow points from the eater to its food.

hint.display: Read the arrow with our three words.

grading.correctAnswerText: False
grading.reason: Right, that is false. The arrow starts at the food and points to the eater.

conceptGroup.goal: Build one forest food chain link by link and draw its arrows
conceptGroup.title: Grass, Deer, Tiger

visual.title: Let's Build One Chain
visual.description: One food chain built link by link - grass, deer, tiger - then joined by two arrows that point at the eater.

question.prompt: Choose all the sentences that follow our arrow rule.

options.text: An arrow runs from the grass to the deer.
An arrow runs from the deer to the tiger.
An arrow runs from the tiger to the deer.
Every arrow points towards the one eating.
Every arrow points towards the food.

hint.display: Eaten first, eater second.

grading.correctAnswerText: An arrow runs from the grass to the deer.; An arrow runs from the deer to the tiger.; Every arrow points towards the one eating.
grading.reason: Yes! Every arrow starts at the food and points to the eater.

conceptGroup.goal: Build one forest food chain link by link and draw its arrows
conceptGroup.title: Grass, Deer, Tiger

visual.title: Let's Build One Chain
visual.description: One food chain built link by link - grass, deer, tiger - then joined by two arrows that point at the eater.

lines.display: A forest does not hold only one chain.
It holds many chains.
Many chains share the same living things.
Their arrows cross over each other.
All those crossing chains together are called a **food web**.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: A Forest Holds Many Chains

cards.title: Why Not Just One Long Chain?

lines.display: Now, why does nature make webs and not just chains?
You might think each animal eats one thing only.
The cow has grass, and the tiger has deer.
Then a web would be just one long chain.
Let's check that.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Why Not Just One Long Chain?

lines.display: Write down everything you ate today.
Roti, dal, milk, a banana, an egg.
That is already a list, not one item.
So you do not eat one thing only.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Check It on Yourself

lines.display: Now watch one crow from your window for ten minutes.
The same crow picks up a thrown-out piece of roti.
Then it pulls an insect out of the ground.
Then it pecks at a fruit.
One crow, three different foods.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Watch One Crow

lines.display: Hardly any animal sticks to one food.
So one animal sits in more than one chain.
That is why the chains cross.
And the crossing is what makes it a web.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: So the Chains Cross

lines.display: Let's follow one path through our forest web.
Grass is eaten by the deer.
The deer is eaten by the tiger.
That is our first path.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: One Path Through the Web

lines.display: Now the second path.
Grass is eaten by the rabbit.
The rabbit is eaten by the snake.
That is a different chain.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: A Second Path

lines.display: Look carefully at the grass.
Two animals eat it, the deer and the rabbit.
So two chains meet right there at the grass.
That is one living thing with two chains crossing at it.
Do that a few more times and you have a web.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Where the Two Paths Meet

lines.display: One more eater belongs in the web.
People forget this one.
A **vulture** does not catch a living animal.
It feeds on the remains of dead animals.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Eater People Forget

lines.display: A deer in our forest dies.
The vulture eats what is left of it.
So an arrow runs from the dead deer to the vulture.
Read it the same way.
The dead deer is eaten by the vulture.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Vulture's Place

question.prompt: A vulture does not catch a living animal. It feeds on the remains of ___.

hint.display: Think about what was left of the deer in our forest.

grading.correctAnswerText: dead animals
grading.reason: Yes! A vulture feeds on the remains of dead animals.

question.prompt: Which of these are true about our forest web?

options.text: The deer and the rabbit both eat the grass.
Two chains cross at the grass.
The vulture eats what is left of the dead deer.
Every animal in the web eats one food only.
The rabbit is eaten by the tiger.

hint.display: Look at the one living thing that two animals eat.

grading.correctAnswerText: The deer and the rabbit both eat the grass.; Two chains cross at the grass.; The vulture eats what is left of the dead deer.
grading.reason: Yes! The chains cross at the grass, and the vulture takes the remains.

lines.display: Now walk back down our chain.
Tiger, then deer, then grass.
The tiger ate the deer.
The deer ate the grass.
And the grass is a plant.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Walk Back Down the Chain

cards.title: Every Chain Starts With a Plant

lines.display: Walk back down any chain and you reach a plant.
A plant at the start, every single time.
So in the end every animal depends on plants.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Every Chain Starts With a Plant

lines.display: Remember **directly** and **indirectly** from the start?
Here they are again.
The deer takes its plant food directly.
The tiger takes plant food indirectly, through the deer.
That same give-and-take runs all over the forest.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Directly and Indirectly, Again

lines.display: This shows us one more thing.
Every living thing in the web matters.
While they are all there, each one has food.
And each one is food for the next.
The whole web keeps working.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Every Living Thing Matters

lines.display: That steady working order has a name.
We call it the **balance of nature**.
Now take one living thing out.
Every chain that ran through it is broken.

visual.title: The Balance of Nature
visual.description: A small forest web of five named living things joined by arrows, with one taken out so the chains through it break.

interactive.label: Tap one living thing to take it out of the web

question.prompt: A tiger eats a deer, and the deer ate grass. How does the tiger get plant food?

options.text: It does not need plant food

hint.display: The plant food went into the deer first.

grading.correctAnswerText: Indirectly, through the deer
grading.reason: Yes! The tiger takes plant food indirectly, through the deer.

question.prompt: Take the grass out of our forest. Choose all the things that would happen.

options.text: The deer would have nothing to eat.
Then the tiger would have nothing to eat.
Every chain through the grass would break.
Nothing in the forest would change.

hint.display: Walk up the chain, one link at a time.

grading.correctAnswerText: The deer would have nothing to eat.; Then the tiger would have nothing to eat.; Every chain through the grass would break.
grading.reason: Yes! One living thing gone, and its chains break. That is the balance of nature.

lines.display: Take the grass away from our forest.
The deer has nothing to eat.
Then the tiger has nothing to eat either.
So each living thing has its own part in that balance.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Take the Grass Away

lines.display: Now the last question of our lesson.
Where do young animals come from?
Look at three sights you know well.
A hen walking with her chicks behind her.
A cat with her kittens.
A nest with eggs sitting in it.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Where Young Animals Come From

lines.display: Every living thing makes new young ones of its own kind.
A hen's young one is a chick.
That chick grows into a hen, never into a kitten.
The young one is always the same sort as its parent.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Of Its Own Kind

lines.display: Making new young ones of its own kind has a name.
We call it **reproduction**.
We met that word with plants.
It is the same idea here with animals.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Reproduction

lines.display: Why does this matter so much?
Suppose one kind of animal stopped making young ones.
The old ones would grow old and die.
No new ones would come.
After some time there would be none of that kind left.
That is why every kind must make its young ones.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Why This Matters So Much

lines.display: Animals do this in two ways.
Only two ways.
Some animals lay eggs.
Some animals give birth to young ones.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Two Ways, Only Two

lines.display: So we have one question to ask about any animal.
Does it lay eggs, or are its young born alive?
One question, two answers.
We will use it for the rest of our lesson.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Our One Question

lines.display: Let's follow an egg from the day it is laid.
A hen lays an egg in her nest.
What happens inside it now?

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one egg from the day it is laid to the day it hatches
conceptGroup.title: From Egg to Chick

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Follow One Egg

lines.display: On the day the egg is laid, the baby is not ready.
There is no finished chick in there.
Not yet.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one egg from the day it is laid to the day it hatches
conceptGroup.title: From Egg to Chick

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Day One: Not Ready Yet

lines.display: The baby grows on inside the egg.
This takes many days.
Every day it grows a little more.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one egg from the day it is laid to the day it hatches
conceptGroup.title: From Egg to Chick

visual.title: The Baby Grows Inside
visual.description: One egg with a marker travelling from laid to ready while the baby inside grows a little more each step.

interactive.label: Move the dot from LAID to READY

lines.display: When the baby is ready, it breaks out itself.
It pushes until the **shell** cracks open.
Then the baby comes out.
We call this **hatching**.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one egg from the day it is laid to the day it hatches
conceptGroup.title: From Egg to Chick

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Breaking Out

cards.title: On the Day It Is Laid

question.prompt:
True or false?

A finished chick sits inside the egg from the first day.

hint.display: Think about the very first day, before the days of growing.

grading.correctAnswerText: False
grading.reason: Right, that is false. The baby is not ready yet. It grows inside first.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one egg from the day it is laid to the day it hatches
conceptGroup.title: From Egg to Chick

question.prompt: Which of these are true about an egg?

options.text: The baby is not ready on the day it is laid.
The baby grows on inside the egg for many days.
When it is ready, the baby breaks out itself.
The parent cracks the shell open for the baby.

hint.display: Remember who does the pushing when the shell cracks.

grading.correctAnswerText: The baby is not ready on the day it is laid.; The baby grows on inside the egg for many days.; When it is ready, the baby breaks out itself.
grading.reason: Yes! It grows inside, then it breaks out itself. We call that hatching.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow one egg from the day it is laid to the day it hatches
conceptGroup.title: From Egg to Chick

lines.display: Now, here is a picture many children hold.
It is worth fixing.
You might think a finished baby bird sits inside the egg.
Curled up in there from the very first day.
Just waiting to push the door open.
It is not like that.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: A Picture Worth Fixing

lines.display: Take an egg from the kitchen.
Crack it into a bowl.
That egg came from a hen.
What is inside?
Only yellow and white.
No ready-made chick anywhere.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Crack an Egg Open

lines.display: Now watch a pigeon's eggs on a ledge.
They lie there for many days.
A parent sits on them all that time.
Only then does anything hatch.
The baby needs all those days to grow.
That is why the parent waits.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Watch a Pigeon's Eggs

cards.title: So the Baby Is Not Ready

lines.display: So the baby is not ready when the egg is laid.
It grows inside, day by day.
And only then does it break out.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: So the Baby Is Not Ready

lines.display: What is the parent doing all that time?
Most egg-laying parents stay close.
They guard their eggs.
Most of them, but not all of them.
Some egg layers leave their eggs and go away.
We will meet those ones at the end of our lesson.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: What the Parent Does

lines.display: So which animals lay eggs?
Here they are.
Birds, insects, fish, frogs, snakes and crocodiles.
All of these lay eggs.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Which Animals Lay Eggs

cards.title: Try the Question on a Hen

lines.display: Let's try our question on one animal you know.
A hen.
Does a hen lay eggs?
Yes, and you have seen them.
So a hen is an egg layer.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Try the Question on a Hen

lines.display: Now try a dog.
Have you ever seen a dog's egg?
No, never.
A dog's puppies are born alive.
So a dog is not an egg layer.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Now Try a Dog

question.prompt: Birds, insects, fish, frogs, snakes and crocodiles all ___.

hint.display: Ask our one question about all of them.

grading.correctAnswerText: lay eggs
grading.reason: Yes! All of them lay eggs. That is one of our two answers.

question.prompt: Choose all the animals that lay eggs.

hint.display: First ask which group each animal is in. Then check our list.

grading.correctAnswerText: A pigeon; An ant; A butterfly
grading.reason: Yes! A pigeon is a bird. An ant and a butterfly are insects. A cow and a cat give birth to young ones.

lines.display: That is the other answer to our question.
Some animals do not lay eggs at all.
Their young ones are born alive.
We call these animals **mammals**.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Other Answer

lines.display: You know many mammals already.
Dogs, cats, cows and monkeys.
And people, because you are a mammal too.
Born alive, not hatched out of an egg.
That is the whole meaning of the word.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Mammals You Know

lines.display: Let's follow a mammal's young one from the start.
Where does it grow, and what does it live on?
Four small steps, and we have it.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow a mammal's young one from before birth until it can feed itself
conceptGroup.title: A Mammal's Young One

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Follow a Mammal's Young One

lines.display: Before it is born, the young one grows inside its mother.
It grows inside her body.
That place is called the **womb**.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow a mammal's young one from before birth until it can feed itself
conceptGroup.title: A Mammal's Young One

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Before It Is Born

lines.display: Then the young one is born.
It comes out alive.
It is already a small animal.
No egg, no shell, no hatching.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow a mammal's young one from before birth until it can feed itself
conceptGroup.title: A Mammal's Young One

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Born Alive

lines.display: The young one cannot eat solid food yet.
So it drinks its mother's **milk**.
Milk is its only food at first.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow a mammal's young one from before birth until it can feed itself
conceptGroup.title: A Mammal's Young One

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: It Drinks Milk

cards.title: Until It Can Eat for Itself

lines.display: It lives on that milk for some time.
It drinks until it is big enough to eat food itself.
A puppy does this, and a kitten does this.
A calf does this, and you did this too.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow a mammal's young one from before birth until it can feed itself
conceptGroup.title: A Mammal's Young One

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Until It Can Eat for Itself

lines.display: Let's see that whole journey in one look.
The young one grows inside its mother, in the womb.
Then it is born alive, already a small animal.
It drinks its mother's milk.
And it grows until it can eat food for itself.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow a mammal's young one from before birth until it can feed itself
conceptGroup.title: A Mammal's Young One

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: That Whole Journey Again

question.prompt: In a mammal's journey, which step comes right after 'Born'?

hint.display: The young one cannot eat solid food yet.

grading.correctAnswerText: Milk
grading.reason: Yes! After it is born, the young one drinks its mother's milk.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow a mammal's young one from before birth until it can feed itself
conceptGroup.title: A Mammal's Young One

question.prompt: Which of these are true about a mammal's young one?

options.text: It grows inside its mother, in the womb.
It drinks its mother's milk at first.
It hatches out of a shell.

hint.display: Think about where the young one grows before it is born.

grading.correctAnswerText: It grows inside its mother, in the womb.; It is born alive.; It drinks its mother's milk at first.
grading.reason: Yes! It grows in the womb, is born alive, and drinks milk.

conceptGroup.goal: Follow a mammal's young one from before birth until it can feed itself
conceptGroup.title: A Mammal's Young One

lines.display: Some animals look like they break our rule.
You might think a bat is a bird, because it flies.
Or that a whale is a fish, because it swims.
Let's test them.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Animals That Look Like Exceptions

cards.title: Flying and Swimming Are Not the Question

lines.display: Flying and swimming are the first things you notice.
But flying and swimming are not our question.
Our question is about the young one.
Does it lay eggs, or are its young born alive?

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Flying and Swimming Are Not the Question

lines.display: A hen's chick comes out of an egg.
You can see those eggs in the coop.
So a hen is an egg layer.
A kitten is born alive.
It pushes in to drink its mother's milk.
So a cat is a mammal.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Two Easy Ones First

lines.display: Now look up into a peepal tree at dusk.
Bats hang there.
A baby bat clings to its mother's body.
It drinks her milk.
There is no nest in that tree.
There is no egg anywhere in it.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Look Up at the Bats

cards.title: So a Bat Is a Mammal

lines.display: So a bat's young one is born alive.
And it lives on milk.
A bat is a mammal, not a bird.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: So a Bat Is a Mammal

lines.display: A whale and a dolphin swim in the sea.
But their young ones are born alive too.
And they drink their mother's milk.
So they are mammals as well, not fish.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: The Whale and the Dolphin

lines.display: Flying decides nothing.
Swimming decides nothing.
Only the young one decides.
Make this a habit from now on.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Only the Young One Decides

lines.display: Whenever an animal looks like it breaks our rule, ask.
Does it lay eggs, or are its young born alive?
Then say your reason out loud.
A hen lays eggs, so a hen is an egg layer.
A cow's calf is born alive and drinks milk.
So a cow is a mammal, and so are dogs and cats.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Say Your Reason Out Loud

question.prompt:
True or false?

A whale is a fish, because it swims in the sea.

hint.display: Swimming is not our question. Ask about the young one.

grading.correctAnswerText: False
grading.reason: Right, that is false. Its young one is born alive and drinks milk. So a whale is a mammal.

question.prompt: An animal flies. Its young one is born alive and drinks milk. What is it?

hint.display: Flying decides nothing. Only the young one decides.

grading.correctAnswerText: A mammal
grading.reason: Yes! Its young one is born alive, so it is a mammal. Think of the bat.

cards.title: Who Looks After the Young Ones

lines.display: One last thing in our lesson.
After the young one arrives, who takes care of it?
Birds and mammals both look after their young ones.
They do it for a long time.
Much longer than other animals do.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Who Looks After the Young Ones

lines.display: Birds and mammals are together on this.
Both of them stay.
Both of them care.
Neither one is ahead of the other.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Together on This

lines.display: Here is what a parent bird does.
It builds a **nest** first, before the eggs come.
Its chicks hatch with no feathers on them.
So they feel cold.
The parent sits over them and keeps them warm.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: What a Parent Bird Does

lines.display: The parent bird also brings food.
It flies off and finds the food.
Then it brings that food back to the nest.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: And It Brings Food

lines.display: Here is what a mammal parent does.
Its young ones drink their mother's milk.
We saw that a moment ago.
And the parent goes on looking after them.
The care does not stop the day the young one is born.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: What a Mammal Parent Does

lines.display: Not every animal looks after its young.
A snake, a turtle and a frog lay their eggs.
They lay them in a safe place.
Then they go away.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Not Every Animal Does This

lines.display: They do not stay with the eggs.
They do not bring food.
Those young ones manage on their own.
Remember what we said about egg-laying parents?
Most guard their eggs, but not all of them.
These three are the ones that do not.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: They Do Not Stay

cards.title: The Ones That Do Not Stay

question.prompt: Snakes, turtles and frogs lay their eggs in a safe place. Then they ___.

hint.display: Not every animal looks after its young ones.

grading.correctAnswerText: go away
grading.reason: Yes! They lay them in a safe place, then go away.

question.prompt: Which of these are true about parents and their young ones?

options.text: Birds and mammals both care for their young a long time.
A parent bird brings food back to the nest.
A mammal's young ones drink their mother's milk.
Mammals look after their young more than birds do.
A frog stays with its eggs and brings them food.

hint.display: Think about what each parent actually does.

grading.correctAnswerText: Birds and mammals both care for their young a long time.; A parent bird brings food back to the nest.; A mammal's young ones drink their mother's milk.
grading.reason: Yes! Birds and mammals both stay and care. Neither one is ahead of the other.

cards.title: Look What You Can Do Now

lines.display: Look what you can do now.
You can say how plants and animals give and take.
Neither side could live without the other.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: Look What You Can Do Now

lines.display: You can put any animal into its feeding group.
Just ask what it eats.
Plant food, flesh, or both.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: You Can Sort Any Animal

lines.display: You can build a food chain and read a food web.
And you know that every chain starts at a plant.
So every animal depends on plants in the end.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: You Can Build a Chain

cards.title: You Can Say How a Young One Arrives

lines.display: You can say how a young one arrives.
It hatches out of an egg, or it is born alive.
And you can say who looks after it.

visual.description: A pencil board drawn with the voice: You Can Say How a Young One Arrives

lines.display: That is a whole chapter about animal life.
And you have it.
Now go and look at the animals around you.
The cow, the crow, the gecko on the wall.
The bee at the flower.
You know their story now.
